explanations.explanation: Twilight, that dim stretch when the day winds down. The LORD says to offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight (Numbers 28:4). So the day gets an offering at each end, with the same grain offering and drink offering both times (Numbers 28:8). Very organized, and I respect a good schedule.

Noon is a fair guess, since it's the middle of the day. But the lambs sit at the two ends of the day: one in the morning and the other at twilight (Numbers 28:4). Think of twilight as the day's last call. The middle of the day doesn't get a lamb here.

Midnight is a long way off, friend. The text says the other lamb is offered at twilight (Numbers 28:4), when the day is winding down. I've spent plenty of nights awake in the dark, so I get why it sounds possible. Still, twilight is the time the verse gives.

Yes, every day. The LORD calls this pair of lambs a regular burnt offering "each day" (Numbers 28:3). Feast days get their own offerings later, but those are added on top. The daily pair is the steady rhythm underneath it all. Steady like my oven timer, which has never once asked for a day off.

Close, but the text says otherwise. The LORD calls the two lambs a regular burnt offering "each day" (Numbers 28:3), not only on special days. The feast days come later in the passage, and their offerings are added on top. So the daily pair keeps going while the calendar fills up around it.

Sinai it is. Verse 6 says this regular burnt offering was "…established at Mount Sinai…" So it's been around since Sinai, not something brand new. Some things have a long history. Mine starts with a 25 cent price sticker in a bakery bin.

Carmel is a good mountain name, but it isn't the one in the text. Verse 6 says this regular burnt offering was established at Mount Sinai. It's the only mountain the verse names. I guessed wrong on things way smaller than mountains back in my drawer days, so no shame here, friend.

Zion is a famous name, so I see why it jumped out. It's the celebrity of mountains, the one everybody's heard of. But verse 6 says this regular burnt offering was "…established at Mount Sinai…" Zion didn't make the guest list for this verse, friend. Sinai is the one.

That sounds tidy, but it's not how the text puts it. The Sabbath offering is "…in addition to the regular burnt offering and its drink offering." (Numbers 28:10). So the daily lambs keep going, and the Sabbath pair is added on top. Nothing gets swapped out.

That's right, nothing gets replaced. The Sabbath offering is "…in addition to the regular burnt offering and its drink offering." (Numbers 28:10). So a Sabbath has the morning lamb, the twilight lamb and the two Sabbath lambs. That's four lambs by my count, and I counted twice on my mustache to be sure.

New moon, yes. Verse 11 puts this offering at "…the beginning of every month…" and verse 14 says it's made "…at each new moon throughout the year." So the month starts with a big offering. Look up at the night sky and you've got a calendar.

Both are moons, so the mix-up is easy. But verse 14 says this is "…the monthly burnt offering to be made at each new moon throughout the year." The text names the new moon. The full moon doesn't come up.

Stars are a fine guess for a sky clue, but the text goes with the moon. Verse 14 says the monthly offering is made "…at each new moon throughout the year." Stars I know a little about, since in my sky every finished cookie box lights one up. This offering, though, goes by the new moon.

A male goat. Verse 15 says it's presented to the LORD as a sin offering. It comes in addition to the regular burnt offering with its drink offering. So the goat has its own job apart from the bulls, the ram and the lambs.

Doves are close to my heart, because Minty, one of my cookie cutter kids, is shaped like one. But verse 15 says one male goat is the sin offering here. The dove doesn't make this list. Sorry, Minty, not this time.

A calf makes sense, since young bulls are already on the list. But those young bulls belong to the burnt offering in verse 11. The sin offering in verse 15 is one male goat. Different animal, different job.

Unleavened bread, the whole week. Verse 17 says the feast is on the fifteenth day, and "for seven days unleavened bread is to be eaten." Unleavened means bread made without leaven. As a cookie man, I respect any dough that doesn't rise.

Grain does show up in this passage, but not as the feast food. Verse 17 says "for seven days unleavened bread is to be eaten." The new grain comes later, with the day of firstfruits (Numbers 28:26). For this seven day feast, it's bread without leaven.
Manna is a famous food, but this passage doesn't name it here. Verse 17 says "for seven days unleavened bread is to be eaten." So the answer is the bread. Stick with what the verse lists, friend.

True. Verse 18 says, "On the first day there is to be a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work." So the feast opens with a sacred assembly and the regular work put down. A whole day off from regular work? I'd need a lie-down just thinking about a day away from my ovens.

The text says it plainly. Verse 18 reads, "On the first day there is to be a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work." So the feast opens with a gathering and a pause from regular work. A fair thing to doubt, but it holds up.

Another sacred assembly, yes. Verse 25 says, "On the seventh day you shall hold a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work." The first day opens with one, and the seventh day has one too. That's a lot of gathering for one feast.

A census is a big deal in a book called Numbers, so I see the pull. But verse 25 says the seventh day is for a sacred assembly, with no regular work. No counting is mentioned there. The text keeps it to the assembly.

A march sounds dramatic, I'll give you that. But verse 25 says, "On the seventh day you shall hold a sacred assembly…" No laps around the camp are mentioned. The final day is for gathering and resting from regular work.

Grain, baker! Verse 26 says, "On the day of firstfruits, when you present an offering of new grain to the LORD during the Feast of Weeks…" As a cookie guy, I respect anything that starts with new grain. The day also comes with a sacred assembly and no regular work, so that's a day off AND an offering of new grain. Nice.
Wine does appear in this passage, but as the drink offering (Numbers 28:14). The firstfruits offering is something else. Verse 26 says it's an offering of new grain.
Oil does appear in this passage, mixed in with the fine flour for the grain offerings (Numbers 28:5). But the firstfruits offering is its own thing. Verse 26 says it's an offering of new grain.

Trumpets, friend. Verse 1 says, "This will be a day for you to sound the trumpets." It's a sacred assembly on the first day of the seventh month, and it comes with a sound you can hear. That's one day nobody could call quiet.

Ruby, one of my cookie cutter kids, is shaped like a bell, so I wish I could say bells. But verse 1 says, "This will be a day for you to sound the trumpets." Trumpets are the instrument the verse gives.
Cymbals are loud, so I see why you went there. But verse 1 says, "This will be a day for you to sound the trumpets." That's the instrument named. It's a trumpet kind of day.

It makes sense on paper, but the text says otherwise. Verse 6 says, "These are in addition to the monthly and daily burnt offerings with their prescribed grain offerings and drink offerings." So nothing gets replaced. The day's offering stacks on top of the others.

That's right, it stacks. Verse 6 says, "These are in addition to the monthly and daily burnt offerings with their prescribed grain offerings and drink offerings." So the first day of the seventh month gets its own offering on top of the others. That's a day I'd need three extra timers just to read about.
Humble. Verse 7 says, "…you shall humble yourselves; you must not do any work." The text doesn't spell out how, so I won't guess. It does say there's a sacred assembly that day.
Washing is a reasonable guess, but the verse doesn't mention it. Verse 7 says, "…you shall humble yourselves…" The text doesn't spell out how, so I'll leave it right there.
Anointing sounds official, I'll give you that. But verse 7 says, "…you shall humble yourselves; you must not do any work." Anointing isn't in that verse. The word the text gives is humble.

Seven days, friend! Verse 12 says, "…you shall observe a feast to the LORD for seven days." That matches the feast after Passover (Numbers 28:17). Seven whole days of feasting is a party I'd need extra cookie boxes for. Hold onto that thought, because verse 35 has one more day waiting at the end.
Three days would be a quick one, but the text gives more. Verse 12 says, "…you shall observe a feast to the LORD for seven days." That's the same length as the feast after Passover. Seven it is.
Forty days is a long feast, friend. Verse 12 says, "…you shall observe a feast to the LORD for seven days." That's the number the text gives. I'd have to stock a lot more cookie boxes for forty.

It would be a quick return, but the text adds one more day. Verse 35 says, "On the eighth day you are to hold a solemn assembly; you must not do any regular work." So the seven days end, and the eighth day is another day of rest from regular work. The calendar isn't done yet.

False, and you caught it! Verse 35 says, "On the eighth day you are to hold a solemn assembly; you must not do any regular work." So you finish the seven days of feast, you figure it's back to work, and the eighth day is still waiting. I'd take that deal every time. On that eighth day, the regular work waits.

Vow and freewill offerings, yes. Verse 39 says these scheduled offerings are "…in addition to your vow and freewill offerings…" So the calendar doesn't use up what people want to bring on their own. That's a nice thing to leave room for.

Guilt and ordination offerings sound serious, and I get why you went there. But verse 39 says these scheduled offerings come "…in addition to your vow and freewill offerings…" The ones you picked just aren't in that verse. So the answer is vow and freewill offerings, which the text puts alongside the scheduled ones.

Those sound official, but this verse doesn't name them. Verse 39 says "…in addition to your vow and freewill offerings…" The text then adds burnt, grain, drink and peace offerings. Wave and heave aren't in that list.

True. Verse 40 says, "So Moses spoke all this to the Israelites just as the LORD had commanded him." Moses, Israel's leader, passes it on just as he was told. Nothing added and nothing trimmed, and that's how I like my recipes.

It's true, and the last verse says so. Verse 40 reads, "So Moses spoke all this to the Israelites just as the LORD had commanded him." Moses, Israel's leader, passes it on just as he was told. After a list that long, a little doubt is understandable.
